newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Nuclear watchdog chief accuses N.Korea of cover-up.
newsitem.headline: Nuclear watchdog chief accuses N.Korea of cover-up.

text.p: North Korea is hiding a stash of plutonium, but evidence to prove it may be slipping away, the head of a United Nations nuclear watchdog said on Tuesday.

Plutonium is the key to a nuclear weapon. Yet Hans Blix stressed that the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) was not asserting that the Stalinist state, which is on the verge of famine, had a nuclear device.

Widespread fears that Pyongyang possessed an atomic bomb were stoked last month when a top North Korean defector warned that his country could turn South Korea into a "sea of fire" -- and scorch Japan -- in a nuclear attack.
The warning by Hwang Jang-yop sent shudders through South Korea, still technically at war with its hostile neighbour since only a truce ended the 1950-53 Korean conflict.
Blix told a news conference that North Korea had more plutonium than it admitted when it signed an agreement with the United States in 1994 to freeze its nuclear programme.
"We have never said -- and we don't know -- how much more than a few hundred grammes (a few ounces) they have," he said, referring to the quantity that Pyongyang declared.
The IAEA director general noted that some countries put the amount at eight kg (17.6 lbs), enough for one bomb.
Nevertheless, he said: "We have never contended that there is a nuclear device for explosive purposes."

Under the 1994 agreement, Pyongyang agreed to scrap its existing Soviet-era nuclear reactor and, later, allow verification of its stock of plutonium during the construction of two safer light-water reactors it was promised.
Such verification would not be made for several years, Blix said. In the meantime, the IAEA was seeking agreement with North Korea on how to preserve the evidence.

But in discussions with North Korean officials on ensuring the truth was not lost, Blix said: "We have not been able to get anywhere at all. That issue remains outstanding, and that is the main issue on which I have expressed concern."
On the bright side, Blix said verification of the nuclear freeze had been "tolerably good". IAEA inspectors are monitoring the decommissioning of the graphite reactor at Yongbyon.

The IAEA raised international alarm in 1993 when it announced its findings of missing plutonium after its first inspection following Pyongyang's agreement to sign the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty and a safeguards pact in 1992.
Nuclear experts have speculated that plutonium may have been extracted from the Yongyon reactor when it was shut down briefly in 1989.
Separately, Blix said China may be ready to step in to resolve a row between Taipei and Seoul over planned shipments of nuclear waste from Taiwan to North Korea.
Last Saturday, Taiwan Power Company said it would press ahead with plans to ship up to 200,000 barrels of waste to the North under a commercial agreement worth some $230 million.

"One avenue being looked into by various parties is that China would take the waste," said Blix, who has just visited the country. He said it was his "definite impression" that China would take the material.
"But whether agreement can be reached, I don't know."

South Korea argues that impoverished North Korea does not have the know-how to safely store the waste. The environmental group Greenpeace has alleged the waste is far more dangerous than Taiwan Power has admitted.
Blix noted widespread concerns about "the transparency of safety aspects of the operation", but stressed the IAEA had no mandate to supervise waste shipments.
